λ<sub>c</sub> = 1.24/E<sub>g</sub> µm (E<sub>g</sub> in eV): Si 1.11 µm, InGaAs 1.65 µm, Ge 1.88 µm; no response beyond it.
I<sub>p</sub> = RP, the current before any avalanche gain.
Fraction of the light absorbed per unit length (m⁻¹ or cm⁻¹); power falls as e<sup>−αx</sup>.
η = (1 − r)(1 − e<sup>−αw</sup>), r the surface reflectivity and w the depleted width.
t<sub>tr</sub> = w/v<sub>sat</sub>; transit-time bandwidth f<sub>tr</sub> ≈ 0.44/t<sub>tr</sub>.
f<sub>RC</sub> = 1/(2πR<sub>L</sub>C) with C = ε<sub>r</sub>ε<sub>0</sub>A/w; overall f<sub>3dB</sub> ≈ 1/√(1/f<sub>tr</sub>² + 1/f<sub>RC</sub>²).
M = I<sub>M</sub>/I<sub>p</sub>; empirically M ≈ 1/[1 − (V/V<sub>B</sub>)<sup>n</sup>]; typically 10 to 100.
k = hole ionisation rate ÷ electron ionisation rate: Si 0.02–0.05, InP about 0.5, Ge near 1.
F = kM + (1 − k)(2 − 1/M); multiplied shot noise is 2qI<sub>p</sub>M²FB.
Thermal-limited estimate M<sub>opt</sub> ≈ [4k<sub>B</sub>T/(kqR<sub>L</sub>I<sub>p</sub>)]<sup>1/3</sup>.

SNR = (MI<sub>p</sub>)²/(i<sub>sh</sub>² + i<sub>th</sub>²); thermal-limited SNR ∝ P², shot-limited SNR ∝ P.
NEP = (σ/√B)/R in W/√Hz: the power that gives SNR = 1 in 1 Hz.
B ≈ A/(2πR<sub>f</sub>C<sub>T</sub>); noise current √(4k<sub>B</sub>TB/R<sub>f</sub>).
PIN: P<sub>sens</sub> ≈ Qσ/R; APD: (Q/R)(qFBQ + σ<sub>T</sub>/M); quoted in dBm with its bit rate and BER.
Q = (I<sub>1</sub> − I<sub>0</sub>)/(σ<sub>1</sub> + σ<sub>0</sub>); best threshold I<sub>D</sub> = (σ<sub>0</sub>I<sub>1</sub> + σ<sub>1</sub>I<sub>0</sub>)/(σ<sub>0</sub> + σ<sub>1</sub>).
BER = ½erfc(Q/√2): Q = 6 gives 10⁻⁹, Q = 7.03 gives 10⁻¹².

10 log₁₀(P<sub>2</sub>/P<sub>1</sub>); 10 log₁₀(Q<sub>2</sub>/Q<sub>1</sub>) with fixed noise, 20 log₁₀(Q<sub>2</sub>/Q<sub>1</sub>) when shot-limited; extinction ratio 10 log₁₀[(1 + r<sub>ex</sub>)/(1 − r<sub>ex</sub>)].

takeaways: A photodiode is a current source driven by light: I<sub>p</sub> = RP with R = ηλ/1.24 A/W, and R ≤ λ/1.24 for any diode without gain.
Every material has a cutoff λ<sub>c</sub> = 1.24/E<sub>g</sub>: silicon stops at 1.11 µm, so the 1.3 and 1.55 µm windows need InGaAs or germanium.

A PIN puts a wide depleted i layer where the light is absorbed: η = (1 − r)(1 − e<sup>−αw</sup>) rises with w, but so does the transit time, while the capacitance falls; the best width balances f<sub>tr</sub> and f<sub>RC</sub>.
An APD multiplies the signal by M and the shot noise by M²F, with F = kM + (1 − k)(2 − 1/M); this gives an optimum gain, larger when k is small.

Noise powers add, never rms currents: σ² = i<sub>sh</sub>² + i<sub>th</sub>². A PIN receiver is almost always thermal-noise limited, because shot noise wins only when I<sub>p</sub>R<sub>L</sub> exceeds 2k<sub>B</sub>T/q ≈ 52 mV.
A transimpedance front end gives the low noise of a large R<sub>f</sub> with a bandwidth about A times wider than a high-impedance stage, which is why it is the standard choice.
Sensitivity is the average power for a target BER at a stated bit rate: Qσ/R for a thermal-limited PIN; an APD at its best gain is typically 5 to 10 dB better.

Q = (I<sub>1</sub> − I<sub>0</sub>)/(σ<sub>1</sub> + σ<sub>0</sub>) alone fixes the BER = ½erfc(Q/√2): Q = 6 gives 10⁻⁹ and Q = 7.03 gives 10⁻¹², provided the threshold is set where both levels are Q noise widths away.

Power penalties turn impairments into decibels: 10 log₁₀(Q<sub>2</sub>/Q<sub>1</sub>) with fixed noise, 20 log₁₀(Q<sub>2</sub>/Q<sub>1</sub>) when shot-limited; a BER floor is a different problem that more power cannot fix.
bank_note: Most syllabi pair the PIN and avalanche photodiodes: expect a labelled structure sketch, the derivation of responsivity, and a PIN-versus-APD comparison with one numerical on gain, noise or sensitivity. Where the receiver and BER are taught, the Q-to-BER relation and a sensitivity in dBm are the usual long questions.

bank.q: Define quantum efficiency and responsivity of a photodetector. Derive R = ηqλ/(hc) and explain why the responsivity rises with wavelength and then falls to zero.
outline: η = electrons collected per incident photon
R = I<sub>p</sub>/P
I<sub>p</sub> = q × ηP/(hν) with hν = hc/λ
so R = ηqλ/(hc) = ηλ/1.24, linear in λ
ceiling for η = 1: 0.69 A/W at 0.85 µm, 1.05 A/W at 1.3 µm
beyond λ<sub>c</sub> = 1.24/E<sub>g</sub> no absorption, R = 0
answer: Quantum efficiency: η = (number of electrons collected per second)/(number of photons arriving per second). It has no units and lies between 0 and 1; a good PIN photodiode has η ≈ 0.7 to 0.9. It is less than 1 because some light is reflected at the surface, some passes through the absorbing layer, and some pairs recombine before they are collected.
Responsivity: R = I<sub>p</sub>/P, the primary photocurrent I<sub>p</sub> (in A) per watt of optical power P falling on the detector. Its unit is A/W.

answer.text: Derivation. Each photon carries energy hν = hc/λ, so a power P is a stream of P/(hν) photons per second. A fraction η of them gives a collected electron of charge q, so the current is
answer.pre:
I<sub>p</sub> = q × η × P/(hν) = ηqPλ/(hc)
R = I<sub>p</sub>/P = ηqλ/(hc)
With hc/q = (6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3 × 10⁸)/(1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹) = 1.24 × 10⁻⁶ V·m = 1.24 µm·V:
R = ηλ/1.24   (λ in µm, R in A/W)

answer: Why R rises with λ: at a fixed η, one watt of longer-wavelength light contains more photons, because each photon carries less energy. More photons per watt means more electrons per watt, so R grows in proportion to λ.

answer.text: The ceiling. Because η ≤ 1, a PIN or PN photodiode always has R ≤ λ/1.24:

answer: Why R then falls to zero: absorption needs hν ≥ E<sub>g</sub>. Beyond the cutoff wavelength λ<sub>c</sub> = 1.24/E<sub>g</sub> the photons are too weak to lift an electron across the bandgap, the material becomes transparent and η → 0. For silicon (E<sub>g</sub> = 1.12 eV) λ<sub>c</sub> = 1.11 µm; for InGaAs (E<sub>g</sub> = 0.75 eV) λ<sub>c</sub> = 1.65 µm. So the R(λ) curve is a rising line that drops sharply near λ<sub>c</sub> (in a real diode the drop starts slightly before λ<sub>c</sub>, where absorption becomes weak).
Note for an APD: its output current per watt is MR, which can be far above λ/1.24, because each primary electron is multiplied by the gain M. The ceiling applies to the primary current.

Check with numbers: a silicon PIN with η = 0.8 at 0.85 µm and 1 µW receives 4.28 × 10¹² photons per second, collects 3.42 × 10¹² electrons per second and gives 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 3.42 × 10¹² = 0.548 µA, so R = 0.548 A/W, the same as 0.8 × 0.85/1.24 = 0.548 A/W.

bank.q: Draw the structure of a PIN photodiode and explain how the intrinsic layer improves performance. Why is the device reverse biased?
outline: p⁺–i–n⁺ sketch, light entering through a thin p⁺ layer with an antireflection coating
reverse bias depletes the whole i layer
most light absorbed inside the high-field region, so pairs are swept out by drift
high η: η = (1 − r)(1 − e<sup>−αw</sup>)
wide i layer lowers capacitance, which helps the RC bandwidth
the η-versus-transit-time compromise

answer.text: Structure (sketch below): a heavily doped p⁺ layer, a wide undoped intrinsic (i) layer, and a heavily doped n⁺ layer, with metal contacts. Light enters through a thin p⁺ layer that carries an antireflection coating. The diode is reverse biased through a load resistor R<sub>L</sub>, across which the signal voltage appears.

svg.aria: PIN photodiode: p plus, wide intrinsic layer and n plus, light entering from the p side, an electron drifting to n plus and a hole to p plus, reverse bias through a load resistor, and the field high and flat across the i layer.

answer: How it works: an absorbed photon with hν ≥ E<sub>g</sub> creates an electron–hole pair. In the depleted i layer a strong field separates the pair at once; the electron drifts to the n⁺ side and the hole to the p⁺ side. This drift current is the photocurrent.

What the i layer improves. (1) Efficiency: in a plain PN diode the depletion layer is thin, so most light is absorbed in the neutral regions, where pairs move by slow diffusion and many recombine. In the PIN the depleted width w is the whole i layer, chosen so that αw is large, and η = (1 − r)(1 − e<sup>−αw</sup>) is close to 1 − r. (2) Speed: carriers made in the i layer move by fast drift, so there is no slow diffusion tail. (3) Capacitance: C = ε<sub>r</sub>ε<sub>0</sub>A/w is small because w is wide, which raises the RC bandwidth 1/(2πR<sub>L</sub>C).

Why reverse bias: (a) it depletes the whole i layer and makes the field strong enough to move carriers at the saturation velocity; (b) it keeps the dark current small (only thermally generated carriers flow); (c) it makes the output current proportional to the light. Forward bias would inject a large diode current of its own and swamp the photocurrent.

The compromise: a wider i layer raises η and lowers C, but the transit time t<sub>tr</sub> = w/v<sub>sat</sub> grows, so the transit-time bandwidth f<sub>tr</sub> ≈ 0.44/t<sub>tr</sub> falls. The designer picks w so that both bandwidth limits are above what the bit rate needs.

Check with numbers (the InGaAs PIN of the chapter): w = 4 µm, α = 10⁴ cm⁻¹, r = 0.03 give αw = 4 and η = 0.97 × (1 − e<sup>−4</sup>) = 0.952; t<sub>tr</sub> = 4 × 10⁻⁶/6.5 × 10⁴ = 61.5 ps, so f<sub>tr</sub> = 7.15 GHz; C = 0.308 pF with 50 Ω gives f<sub>RC</sub> = 10.35 GHz; together about 5.9 GHz.

bank.q: Explain impact ionisation in an avalanche photodiode. Define the multiplication factor M, the ionisation ratio k and the excess noise factor F, and say why a small k is wanted.
outline: strong field near breakdown accelerates carriers to ionising energy
each ionising collision creates a new pair, giving a chain
M = I<sub>M</sub>/I<sub>p</sub>; M ≈ 1/[1 − (V/V<sub>B</sub>)<sup>n</sup>] rises steeply near breakdown
k = hole rate/electron rate; F = kM + (1 − k)(2 − 1/M)
small k: avalanche carried by one carrier type, low F
typical M = 10 to 100, limited by noise and breakdown
answer: Impact ionisation: in the gain region of an APD the reverse bias makes the field close to the breakdown field. A carrier accelerated there gains, between collisions with the lattice, more energy than the bandgap. When it collides it can lift a valence electron into the conduction band, creating a new electron–hole pair. The new carriers are accelerated too and can ionise again, so one primary pair triggers an avalanche.

In a reach-through APD (n⁺–p–π–p⁺) light is absorbed in the wide, lightly doped π layer at moderate field, and the electrons drift into the thin p layer next to the n⁺ contact, where the field is highest and multiplication happens. In an InGaAs/InP SAM APD, InGaAs absorbs and InP multiplies.

answer.text: Multiplication factor:

answer: Here I<sub>M</sub> is the multiplied output current, I<sub>p</sub> the primary photocurrent, V the bias and V<sub>B</sub> the breakdown voltage. Example: V<sub>B</sub> = 50 V and n = 3 give M = 10 at V = 50 × 0.9<sup>1/3</sup> = 48.3 V, and M = 8.7 at 48 V, so M is very sensitive to bias and to temperature (V<sub>B</sub> rises as the diode warms).

Ionisation ratio: k = β/α, the hole ionisation rate β over the electron ionisation rate α (for an avalanche started by electrons). Silicon: k ≈ 0.02 to 0.05; InP gain region: about 0.5; germanium: near 1.

answer.text: Excess noise factor: the number of secondary pairs per primary pair is random, so the output fluctuates more than plain shot noise. The multiplied shot noise is 2qI<sub>p</sub>M²F(M)B with

answer: Why small k: with k small, only electrons ionise, so the avalanche runs one way across the gain region, ends quickly and is less random. F stays near 2 even at large M, the gain–bandwidth product is higher, and the optimum gain is larger. With k = 1 holes also ionise and travel back, the chain feeds on itself, and F = M.
Check: k = 0.3 and M = 10 give F = 0.3 × 10 + 0.7 × 1.9 = 4.33, the value used in the APD worked example; typical operating gains are M = 10 to 100.

bank.q: State the two main noise currents of an optical receiver and give their mean-square expressions. For a PIN with I<sub>p</sub> = 1 µA, say which dominates at 100 Mb/s (R<sub>L</sub> = 1 kΩ, B = 70 MHz) and at 2.5 Gb/s (R<sub>L</sub> = 200 Ω, B = 1.75 GHz).
outline: shot noise i<sub>sh</sub>² = 2q(I<sub>p</sub> + I<sub>d</sub>)B, from random carrier arrival
thermal noise i<sub>th</sub>² = 4k<sub>B</sub>TB/R<sub>L</sub>, from the load resistor
both mean-square currents in A² within bandwidth B; powers add
ratio i<sub>sh</sub>²/i<sub>th</sub>² = qI<sub>p</sub>R<sub>L</sub>/(2k<sub>B</sub>T), independent of B
thermal noise dominates in both cases, more so at 2.5 Gb/s where R<sub>L</sub> must be small
dark current adds to shot noise; an APD makes shot noise large
answer: Shot noise: the photocurrent and dark current are streams of separate carriers arriving at random times (Poisson statistics). Within the receiver bandwidth B the mean-square fluctuation is i<sub>sh</sub>² = 2q(I<sub>p</sub> + I<sub>d</sub>)B, where q = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, I<sub>p</sub> is the photocurrent and I<sub>d</sub> the dark current. For an APD it becomes 2q(I<sub>p</sub> + I<sub>db</sub>)M²FB + 2qI<sub>ds</sub>B.

Thermal (Johnson) noise: random thermal motion of electrons in the load resistor R<sub>L</sub> gives i<sub>th</sub>² = 4k<sub>B</sub>TB/R<sub>L</sub>, with k<sub>B</sub> = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J/K and T in kelvin. It does not depend on the light. An amplifier noise figure multiplies it.
The two are independent, so their mean squares add: σ² = i<sub>sh</sub>² + i<sub>th</sub>², and SNR = I<sub>p</sub>²/σ².

Which dominates: the ratio is i<sub>sh</sub>²/i<sub>th</sub>² = 2qI<sub>p</sub>B/(4k<sub>B</sub>TB/R<sub>L</sub>) = qI<sub>p</sub>R<sub>L</sub>/(2k<sub>B</sub>T). B cancels, so the answer depends on I<sub>p</sub>R<sub>L</sub>: shot noise wins only when I<sub>p</sub>R<sub>L</sub> > 2k<sub>B</sub>T/q = 51.7 mV at 300 K.

answer.text: Working, with I<sub>p</sub> = 1 µA and T = 300 K:

answer: Conclusion: in a PIN receiver thermal noise dominates in both cases, by a factor of about 50 at 100 Mb/s and about 260 at 2.5 Gb/s. At the higher bit rate the bandwidth needs a smaller R<sub>L</sub> (to keep R<sub>L</sub>C short), and a smaller R<sub>L</sub> makes thermal noise worse. The SNR falls from 29.3 dB to 8.4 dB for the same 1 µA.
Shot noise matters when the current is large or when an APD multiplies it by M²F, and in coherent receivers where a strong local laser raises the current.

With an APD the picture changes. Take the 100 Mb/s case with M = 10 and F = 5: the shot noise is multiplied by M²F = 500, giving 500 × 2.24 × 10⁻¹⁷ = 1.12 × 10⁻¹⁴ A², now 9.7 times the thermal noise of 1.16 × 10⁻¹⁵ A². So an APD receiver can be shot-noise limited even when a PIN receiver with the same front end never is; that is exactly why APD gain has an optimum.
Check: 51.7 mV/1 kΩ = 51.7 µA and 51.7 mV/200 Ω = 259 µA are the photocurrents at which the two noises would be equal; 1 µA is far below both.

bank.q: A silicon PIN photodiode has η = 0.80 and receives 2 µW at λ = 0.85 µm. Find the responsivity and the photocurrent. A germanium diode used at 1.3 µm has η = 0.60. What power gives it the same current?
outline: R = ηqλ/(hc) = ηλ/1.24
constants q = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s, c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s
R = 0.548 A/W at 0.85 µm with η = 0.8
I<sub>p</sub> = RP = 1.10 µA
at 1.3 µm with η = 0.6: R = 0.629 A/W, so P = 1.74 µW
units throughout
answer: Photocurrent: I<sub>p</sub> = RP = 0.548 A/W × 2 × 10⁻⁶ W = 1.097 × 10⁻⁶ A ≈ 1.10 µA.
Check by counting photons: E = hc/λ = 2.339 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, so 2 µW is 8.55 × 10¹² photons per second; 80 % of them give 6.84 × 10¹² electrons per second; × 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C = 1.10 µA.
Germanium at 1.3 µm: silicon cannot be used here (its cutoff is 1.11 µm), but germanium (cutoff 1.88 µm) can. R = 0.60 × 1.30/1.24 = 0.629 A/W.
Power for the same current: P = I<sub>p</sub>/R = 1.097 µA/0.629 A/W = 1.74 µW.

Check by counting photons for germanium: E = hc/λ = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3 × 10⁸/1.3 × 10⁻⁶ = 1.529 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, so 1.74 µW is 1.14 × 10¹³ photons per second; 60 % of them give 6.84 × 10¹² electrons per second, the same electron rate as the silicon diode (80 % of 8.55 × 10¹²), and therefore the same 1.10 µA.
Units: R in A/W is the same number as µA per µW or mA per mW, so the silicon diode gives 0.548 µA for every microwatt; keep λ in micrometres in ηλ/1.24, or in metres in ηqλ/(hc), never mixed.

Comment: the germanium diode needs less power (1.74 µW against 2 µW) even though its η is lower, because at 1.3 µm each watt carries 1.3/0.85 = 1.53 times as many photons. The ratio 0.629/0.548 = 1.148 = (0.60/0.80) × (1.30/0.85) shows both effects.

answer.text: Summary of the working:

answer: Choice of material at 1.3 µm: germanium works, but its small bandgap gives a larger dark current, so InGaAs is the usual choice in fiber receivers. An InGaAs diode with η = 0.8 has R = 0.8 × 1.3/1.24 = 0.839 A/W and would need only 1.097/0.839 = 1.31 µW for the same current.
Check: 0.629 × 1.74 = 1.094 µA ≈ 1.10 µA (rounding), the same current as required.

bank.q: A receiver has load resistance 1 kΩ at 300 K and bandwidth 100 MHz. Calculate the rms thermal noise current. An APD with M = 20 and F = 4 gives a primary photocurrent of 1 µA (dark current negligible). Find the rms shot noise before and after gain, the SNR with and without the gain, and say which noise dominates in each case.
outline: σ<sub>th</sub> = √(4k<sub>B</sub>TB/R<sub>L</sub>) = 40.7 nA
primary shot noise 2qI<sub>p</sub>B = 3.20 × 10⁻¹⁷ A², rms 5.66 nA
with gain the mean square is multiplied by M²F = 1600
rms APD shot noise √(5.13 × 10⁻¹⁴) = 226 nA
signal 20 µA; SNR 38.8 dB with gain against 27.7 dB without
both noises referred to the same point (the photodiode output)
answer: Thermal noise: i<sub>th</sub>² = 4k<sub>B</sub>TB/R<sub>L</sub> = 4 × 1.38 × 10⁻²³ × 300 × 10⁸/10³ = 1.656 × 10⁻¹⁵ A², so σ<sub>th</sub> = √(1.656 × 10⁻¹⁵) = 4.07 × 10⁻⁸ A = 40.7 nA rms.
Primary shot noise (no gain, M = F = 1): i<sub>sh</sub>² = 2qI<sub>p</sub>B = 2 × 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 1 × 10⁻⁶ × 10⁸ = 3.20 × 10⁻¹⁷ A², rms 5.66 nA.

With gain: the mean square is multiplied by M²F = 20² × 4 = 1600, so i<sub>sh</sub>² = 1600 × 3.204 × 10⁻¹⁷ = 5.13 × 10⁻¹⁴ A², rms 226 nA. (The rms grows by √1600 = 40, from 5.66 nA to 226 nA, while the signal grows by M = 20.)
Signal: without gain the signal current is 1 µA; with gain it is MI<sub>p</sub> = 20 µA. Both noise terms are referred to the same point, the photodiode output, so they can be added.

Gain at which the two noises are equal: M²F × 3.204 × 10⁻¹⁷ = 1.656 × 10⁻¹⁵ gives M²F = 51.7; with F = 4 that is M = √(51.7/4) = 3.6. Below about M = 3.6 thermal noise dominates, above it the multiplied shot noise does, so M = 20 is well into the shot-limited region.

answer.text: Working table:

answer: SNR without gain: 1.00 × 10⁻¹²/1.688 × 10⁻¹⁵ = 592, or 27.7 dB. Thermal noise is 52 times the shot noise: thermal-noise limited.
SNR with gain: 4.00 × 10⁻¹⁰/(5.13 × 10⁻¹⁴ + 1.656 × 10⁻¹⁵) = 4.00 × 10⁻¹⁰/5.29 × 10⁻¹⁴ = 7560, or 38.8 dB. Now the multiplied shot noise is 31 times the thermal noise: shot-noise limited.

Interpretation: the gain raised the signal power 400 times (26 dB) but the SNR only 11.1 dB, because the shot noise grew by 1600 times. The receiver has moved past the thermal limit into the shot-limited region, so a higher M would now lower the SNR: the excess noise factor F already costs 10 log₁₀ 4 = 6 dB compared with a noiseless gain.

Check: with gain, if thermal noise were ignored, SNR = (MI<sub>p</sub>)²/(2qI<sub>p</sub>M²FB) = I<sub>p</sub>/(2qFB) = 10⁻⁶/(2 × 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 4 × 10⁸) = 7800 (38.9 dB), only slightly above the full 7560, confirming the shot-noise limit.

bank.q: A receiver has mean levels I<sub>1</sub> = 2 µA and I<sub>0</sub> = 0.2 µA with noise currents σ<sub>1</sub> = σ<sub>0</sub> = 0.15 µA. Find Q, the decision threshold and the bit error rate. What must Q become for a target of 10⁻¹², and how could that be achieved? How many errors per second does each BER give at 2.5 Gbit/s?
outline: Q = (I<sub>1</sub> − I<sub>0</sub>)/(σ<sub>1</sub> + σ<sub>0</sub>) = 1.8/0.30 = 6
equal noise: threshold halfway, 1.1 µA
BER = ½erfc(Q/√2) = 9.9 × 10⁻¹⁰
target 10⁻¹² needs Q = 7.03
raise the gap by 17 % or cut the noise by 15 %; fixed-noise penalty 0.69 dB
errors per second = BER × bit rate
answer: Threshold: the noises are equal, so the best threshold is halfway: I<sub>D</sub> = (σ<sub>0</sub>I<sub>1</sub> + σ<sub>1</sub>I<sub>0</sub>)/(σ<sub>0</sub> + σ<sub>1</sub>) = (I<sub>1</sub> + I<sub>0</sub>)/2 = 1.1 µA. Check: (2.0 − 1.1)/0.15 = 6 and (1.1 − 0.2)/0.15 = 6.
BER: BER = ½erfc(Q/√2) = ½erfc(4.243) = 9.87 × 10⁻¹⁰ ≈ 10⁻⁹. The large-Q form e<sup>−Q²/2</sup>/(Q√(2π)) = e<sup>−18</sup>/(6 × 2.507) = 1.52 × 10⁻⁸/15.04 = 1.01 × 10⁻⁹ agrees within 3 %.
Q for 10⁻¹²: solving ½erfc(Q/√2) = 10⁻¹² gives Q = 7.03 (check: ½erfc(7.03/√2) = 1.0 × 10⁻¹²).

answer.text: How to get there (Q must rise by 7.03/6.0 = 1.172):

head: Change
New value
Comment
rows: Raise the gap I<sub>1</sub> − I<sub>0</sub>, same noise
more optical power; penalty 10 log₁₀ 1.172 = 0.69 dB if the noise is fixed (thermal)
quieter front end or narrower filter
a gap of 2.11 µA with I<sub>1</sub> = 2 µA would need I<sub>0</sub> < 0, so I<sub>0</sub> alone cannot do it

answer: If the noise were shot-limited (σ ∝ √P), Q ∝ √P and the power would have to rise by 1.172² = 1.374, a penalty of 1.38 dB.

The non-zero 0 level also costs power. Here r<sub>ex</sub> = I<sub>0</sub>/I<sub>1</sub> = 0.2/2 = 0.1, so compared with a perfect zero at the same average power the receiver pays 10 log₁₀[(1 + 0.1)/(1 − 0.1)] = 0.87 dB (thermal noise). Raising the extinction ratio of the transmitter is therefore worth almost as much as the 0.69 dB needed for 10⁻¹².

In the eye diagram: the eye opening at the sampling instant is 1.8 µA, and a margin of Qσ = 6 × 0.15 = 0.9 µA must fit above and below the 1.1 µA threshold. For 10⁻¹² each margin must grow to 7.03 × 0.15 = 1.05 µA, so the eye must open to 2.11 µA.

answer.text: Errors per second at 2.5 Gbit/s:
answer.pre:
BER 9.87 × 10⁻¹⁰:  9.87 × 10⁻¹⁰ × 2.5 × 10⁹ = 2.47 errors per second
BER 1.0 × 10⁻¹²:   1.0 × 10⁻¹² × 2.5 × 10⁹ = 0.0025 per second (one every 400 s)

answer: BER depends only on Q, not on the absolute currents: doubling all four currents (I<sub>1</sub>, I<sub>0</sub>, σ<sub>1</sub>, σ<sub>0</sub>) leaves Q = 6 and the BER unchanged.
Check: a gap of 2.11 µA over noise 0.30 µA gives Q = 2.11/0.30 = 7.03, and 1.8/(2 × 0.128) = 7.03 too.

bank.q: A 2.5 Gbit/s receiver at 1.55 µm uses a PIN with R = 0.9 A/W. Its front end adds thermal noise σ<sub>T</sub> = 150 nA rms in a bandwidth B = 1.25 GHz, and it must reach BER 10⁻⁹ (Q = 6). Find the PIN sensitivity. A designer hopes to gain 12 dB by fitting an InGaAs APD (k = 0.5, same R). Using P<sub>sens</sub> = (Q/R)(qFBQ + σ<sub>T</sub>/M), find the best gain and the sensitivity, and comment on the 12 dB hope.
outline: PIN: P<sub>sens</sub> = Qσ<sub>T</sub>/R = 1.00 µW = −30.0 dBm
APD: F = kM + (1 − k)(2 − 1/M); thermal term falls as 1/M, shot term grows with F
tabulate P<sub>sens</sub> against M; best M ≈ 16
best APD sensitivity −38.7 dBm, 8.7 dB better than the PIN
12 dB is not reachable with k = 0.5; a lower-k APD or an optical preamplifier is needed
state the assumptions (zero level zero, Gaussian noise)
answer: Assumptions: on–off keying with a zero level of zero, Gaussian noise, equal ones and zeros; the APD has the same primary responsivity and the same front end; dark current neglected.

PIN sensitivity: P<sub>sens</sub> = Qσ<sub>T</sub>/R = 6 × 150 × 10⁻⁹/0.9 = 1.00 × 10⁻⁶ W = 1.00 µW, which is 10 log₁₀(10⁻⁶/10⁻³) = −30.0 dBm. (Including the small PIN shot term (Q/R)qBQ = 8 nW changes it by only 0.03 dB.)

APD sensitivity: P<sub>sens</sub> = (Q/R)(qFBQ + σ<sub>T</sub>/M). The second term is the thermal noise referred back through the gain; it falls as 1/M. The first is the multiplied shot noise; it grows with F, and F grows with M. With k = 0.5, F = 0.5M + 0.5(2 − 1/M).

Best gain: the minimum is near M = 16 (the formula M<sub>opt</sub> ≈ √[(σ<sub>T</sub>/(QqB) + k − 1)/k] = √[(124.8 − 0.5)/0.5] = 15.8 agrees). There the two terms are of the same size, and the sensitivity is 134 nW = −38.7 dBm.
Improvement: −30.0 − (−38.7) = 8.7 dB. The curve is flat near the optimum: anywhere from M = 10 to M = 20 is within about 0.4 dB of the best, which matters because M drifts with temperature.

What the APD sees at its sensitivity: the average primary photocurrent is RP = 0.9 × 134 nW = 121 nA, multiplied to 16 × 121 nA = 1.93 µA at the output. The PIN at its own sensitivity sees 0.9 µA, but with no gain to lift it above the 150 nA amplifier noise.

The 12 dB hope: not reachable. Raising M beyond 16 makes things worse, because the excess noise grows faster than the thermal term shrinks. With k = 0.5 the best possible gain is 8.7 dB, inside the usual 5 to 10 dB range for APD receivers. To get 12 dB the designer needs a lower-noise APD (a smaller k, for example an InAlAs gain layer), a quieter front end, or an optical preamplifier (an erbium-doped fiber amplifier) before the PIN.

bank.q: A receiver front end uses a transimpedance amplifier with R<sub>f</sub> = 10 kΩ, open-loop gain A = 20 and a total input capacitance of 1 pF. Estimate its bandwidth and compare it with a high-impedance front end using the same resistor. What happens if R<sub>f</sub> is raised to 100 kΩ for better sensitivity, for a 100 Mbit/s NRZ signal?
outline: TIA bandwidth B ≈ A/(2πR<sub>f</sub>C<sub>T</sub>)
10 kΩ, 1 pF, A = 20: about 318 MHz; high impedance only 15.9 MHz
100 kΩ: about 31.8 MHz, below the 50–70 MHz a 100 Mbit/s NRZ signal needs
thermal noise √(4k<sub>B</sub>TB/R<sub>f</sub>) falls by √10
trade-off between thermal noise and speed
equalisation as a partial fix
answer: TIA bandwidth: feedback makes the input look like R<sub>f</sub>/(A + 1), so B ≈ A/(2πR<sub>f</sub>C<sub>T</sub>) = 20/(2π × 10⁴ × 10⁻¹²) = 3.18 × 10⁸ Hz = 318 MHz.

High-impedance front end with R<sub>L</sub> = 10 kΩ: B = 1/(2πR<sub>L</sub>C<sub>T</sub>) = 1/(2π × 10⁴ × 10⁻¹²) = 15.9 MHz, twenty times narrower, so it would integrate the pulses and need an equaliser.

Noise of the 10 kΩ resistor over 100 MHz: √(4k<sub>B</sub>TB/R<sub>f</sub>) = √(4 × 1.38 × 10⁻²³ × 300 × 10⁸/10⁴) = 12.9 nA rms, both for the TIA and the high-impedance case: the TIA gets the low noise of a large resistor without its narrow bandwidth.
What 100 Mbit/s needs: an NRZ signal needs a receiver bandwidth of about 0.5 to 0.7 times the bit rate, 50 to 70 MHz.

answer.text: Raising R<sub>f</sub> to 100 kΩ:

answer: Effect: the noise current falls by √10 = 3.16 (about 5 dB better sensitivity, since P<sub>sens</sub> ∝ σ), but the bandwidth falls ten times to 31.8 MHz. The pulses then spread into their neighbours (intersymbol interference), the eye closes, and the BER rises however quiet the amplifier is.

Options: choose the largest R<sub>f</sub> that still gives about 70 MHz, R<sub>f</sub> ≈ A/(2πBC<sub>T</sub>) = 20/(2π × 7 × 10⁷ × 10⁻¹²) = 45 kΩ; or lower C<sub>T</sub> with a smaller photodiode; or add an equaliser after a slower front end, which restores bandwidth but also boosts high-frequency noise.

Gain from that choice: over a 70 MHz bandwidth the noise of 10 kΩ is √(4k<sub>B</sub>T × 7 × 10⁷/10⁴) = 10.8 nA and that of 45 kΩ is 5.1 nA, so the sensitivity improves by 10 log₁₀(10.8/5.1) = 3.3 dB without losing the bandwidth. This is the usual design rule: make R<sub>f</sub> as large as the bandwidth allows.

Check: 318 MHz × 10 kΩ = 3.18 × 10¹² and 31.8 MHz × 100 kΩ = 3.18 × 10¹², the same product A/(2πC<sub>T</sub>), as expected: bandwidth times R<sub>f</sub> is fixed by the amplifier and the capacitance.

bank.q: Show why an APD has an optimum gain. Derive or state the condition for M<sub>opt</sub> and explain how the ionisation ratio k shifts it, using the APD of the worked example (I<sub>p</sub> = 83.9 nA, B = 1 GHz, R<sub>L</sub> = 1 kΩ, T = 300 K).
outline: SNR = (MI<sub>p</sub>)²/[2qI<sub>p</sub>M²FB + 4k<sub>B</sub>TB/R<sub>L</sub>]
low M: thermal noise dominates, SNR ∝ M²; high M: SNR falls as 1/F
differentiate and set to zero: M<sub>opt</sub> ≈ [4k<sub>B</sub>T/(kqR<sub>L</sub>I<sub>p</sub>)]<sup>1/3</sup>
k = 0.3 gives M<sub>opt</sub> ≈ 16; k = 0.02 about 39; k = 1 about 11
sketch of SNR against M with a broad maximum

answer.text: SNR of an APD receiver (dark current neglected):

answer: Low gain: the thermal term 4k<sub>B</sub>TB/R<sub>L</sub> dominates the denominator, and the numerator grows as M², so SNR ∝ M²: every doubling of M adds 6 dB.
High gain: the shot term dominates; then SNR ≈ I<sub>p</sub>/(2qF(M)B). The M² cancels, but F grows (about kM for large M), so SNR falls as M rises. Between these two regions there must be a maximum.

answer.text: Condition for the maximum: divide top and bottom by M², SNR = I<sub>p</sub>²/[2qI<sub>p</sub>F(M)B + 4k<sub>B</sub>TB/(R<sub>L</sub>M²)]. The SNR is largest when the bracket is smallest. For M ≫ 1 take F ≈ kM + 2(1 − k), so dF/dM ≈ k. Setting the derivative of the bracket to zero:

answer: Meaning of the condition: multiplying it by M³ gives kM × 2qI<sub>p</sub>M²B = 8k<sub>B</sub>TB/R<sub>L</sub>, so at the optimum the gain-dependent part of the shot noise is twice the thermal noise. Beyond M<sub>opt</sub> each extra unit of gain adds more noise power than signal power.

Numbers for the worked example: 4k<sub>B</sub>T = 1.656 × 10⁻²⁰ J; qR<sub>L</sub>I<sub>p</sub> = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 1000 × 83.9 × 10⁻⁹ = 1.344 × 10⁻²³. For k = 0.3: M<sub>opt</sub>³ = 1.656 × 10⁻²⁰/(0.3 × 1.344 × 10⁻²³) = 4108, so M<sub>opt</sub> = 16.0.

answer.text: How k shifts it (exact SNR maximum found numerically from the formula above):
Sketch: SNR against M for three values of k (same I<sub>p</sub>, B, R<sub>L</sub>). All start at −3.7 dB for M = 1 (the PIN value).

svg.aria: SNR in decibels against gain M on a log scale from 1 to 300 for k equals 0.02, 0.3 and 1. All start at minus 3.7 dB; the k 0.02 curve peaks at 19.2 dB near M 39, the k 0.3 curve at 14.9 dB near M 16 and the k 1 curve at 12.1 dB near M 11.

answer: Interpretation: M<sub>opt</sub> ∝ k<sup>−1/3</sup>, so a smaller k allows a larger useful gain and a higher peak SNR; it also rises when the thermal noise is larger (smaller R<sub>L</sub>, higher T) and falls when the photocurrent is larger, because a strong signal already has enough shot noise. The maximum is broad: for k = 0.3 the SNR is within 1 dB of its peak from about M = 10 to M = 25.

bank.q: Discuss the trade-off between quantum efficiency and bandwidth in a photodiode. For the InGaAs PIN of the chapter (α = 10⁴ cm⁻¹, r = 0.03, A = 10⁻⁸ m², ε<sub>r</sub> = 13.9, v<sub>sat</sub> = 6.5 × 10⁴ m/s, R<sub>L</sub> = 50 Ω), find the i-layer width that gives the widest bandwidth and its η.
outline: η = (1 − r)(1 − e<sup>−αw</sup>) wants a large w
transit time w/v<sub>sat</sub> and f<sub>tr</sub> ≈ 0.44v<sub>sat</sub>/w want a small w
C = ε<sub>r</sub>ε<sub>0</sub>A/w falls as w grows, so f<sub>RC</sub> rises with w
best bandwidth where f<sub>tr</sub> = f<sub>RC</sub>: w ≈ 3.3 µm, about 6.1 GHz, η = 0.935
InGaAs needs only a few µm; silicon at 0.85 µm needs tens of µm
waveguide and back-illuminated detectors break the trade-off
answer: Efficiency: η = (1 − r)(1 − e<sup>−αw</sup>). The light must be absorbed within the depleted width w, so η grows with w and saturates at 1 − r once αw is about 3 or more.
Transit time: carriers cross the i layer in t<sub>tr</sub> = w/v<sub>sat</sub>, giving a 3 dB bandwidth f<sub>tr</sub> ≈ 0.44/t<sub>tr</sub> = 0.44v<sub>sat</sub>/w. A wide layer is slow.

RC limit: the depleted layer is a capacitor C = ε<sub>r</sub>ε<sub>0</sub>A/w, giving f<sub>RC</sub> = 1/(2πR<sub>L</sub>C) = w/(2πR<sub>L</sub>ε<sub>r</sub>ε<sub>0</sub>A). A thin layer has a large C and is also slow. The overall bandwidth is about f<sub>3dB</sub> = 1/√(1/f<sub>tr</sub>² + 1/f<sub>RC</sub>²).

answer.text: Working for the chapter's diode:
Best width: f<sub>tr</sub> falls as 1/w and f<sub>RC</sub> rises as w, so the combined bandwidth peaks where they are equal:
answer.pre:
0.44v<sub>sat</sub>/w = w/(2πR<sub>L</sub>ε<sub>r</sub>ε<sub>0</sub>A)
w² = 0.44v<sub>sat</sub> × 2πR<sub>L</sub>ε<sub>r</sub>ε<sub>0</sub>A = 0.44 × 6.5 × 10⁴ × 2π × 50 × 13.9 × 8.85 × 10⁻¹² × 10⁻⁸
w = 3.32 µm, f<sub>tr</sub> = f<sub>RC</sub> = 8.61 GHz, f<sub>3dB</sub> = 8.61/√2 = 6.08 GHz

answer: At that width η = 0.97 × (1 − e<sup>−3.32</sup>) = 0.935, only 1.7 points below the 0.952 of the 4 µm design, while the bandwidth is 0.2 GHz higher. Going thinner costs efficiency fast (w = 1 µm gives η = 0.61) and, here, also costs bandwidth because the capacitance takes over.

Material matters: InGaAs at 1.55 µm (1/α = 1 µm) reaches good η with a few micrometres, so it can be fast. Silicon at 0.85 µm absorbs weakly (α of the order of 10³ cm⁻¹ or less) and needs 20 to 50 µm, so silicon PINs are slower. Reducing the area A lowers C and moves the optimum to a thinner, faster layer, at the price of harder fiber alignment.

Breaking the trade-off: a waveguide photodiode guides the light along the absorbing layer, so the light path is long (good η) while the carrier path across the layer stays short (fast). Back-illuminated designs with a mirror pass the light twice. Uni-travelling-carrier diodes let only the fast electrons cross the depleted region.

Check of the optimum: f<sub>tr</sub> = 0.44 × 6.5 × 10⁴/3.32 × 10⁻⁶ = 8.61 GHz; C = 13.9 × 8.85 × 10⁻¹² × 10⁻⁸/3.32 × 10⁻⁶ = 0.370 pF; f<sub>RC</sub> = 1/(2π × 50 × 0.370 × 10⁻¹²) = 8.60 GHz. Equal, as required.

bank.q: Derive the relation between Q and bit error rate for Gaussian noise. Show why a threshold set midway between I<sub>1</sub> and I<sub>0</sub> is not the best choice when the two noise levels differ, using I<sub>1</sub> = 1.0 µA, I<sub>0</sub> = 0.10 µA, σ<sub>1</sub> = 0.10 µA and σ<sub>0</sub> = 0.05 µA.
outline: the decision compares the sample with a threshold I<sub>D</sub>
BER = ½P(0|1) + ½P(1|0) for equally likely bits
Gaussian tails: P(0|1) = ½erfc[(I<sub>1</sub> − I<sub>D</sub>)/(σ<sub>1</sub>√2)], P(1|0) = ½erfc[(I<sub>D</sub> − I<sub>0</sub>)/(σ<sub>0</sub>√2)]
best threshold makes both arguments equal: I<sub>D</sub> = (σ<sub>0</sub>I<sub>1</sub> + σ<sub>1</sub>I<sub>0</sub>)/(σ<sub>0</sub> + σ<sub>1</sub>)
then Q = (I<sub>1</sub> − I<sub>0</sub>)/(σ<sub>1</sub> + σ<sub>0</sub>) and BER = ½erfc(Q/√2)
numbers: best I<sub>D</sub> = 0.40 µA gives 9.9 × 10⁻¹⁰; halfway 0.55 µA gives 1.7 × 10⁻⁶
answer: Model: at the sampling instant a 1 bit gives a current with mean I<sub>1</sub> and rms noise σ<sub>1</sub>; a 0 bit gives mean I<sub>0</sub> and noise σ<sub>0</sub>. The noise is Gaussian. The decision circuit says 1 if the sample exceeds the threshold I<sub>D</sub>. Ones and zeros are equally likely.

answer.text: Error probabilities: a 1 is lost if its sample falls below I<sub>D</sub>; a 0 is wrong if its sample rises above I<sub>D</sub>. For a Gaussian, the tail beyond a distance d is ½erfc(d/(σ√2)), so
answer.pre:
P(0|1) = ½ erfc[(I<sub>1</sub> − I<sub>D</sub>)/(σ<sub>1</sub>√2)]
P(1|0) = ½ erfc[(I<sub>D</sub> − I<sub>0</sub>)/(σ<sub>0</sub>√2)]
BER = ½P(0|1) + ½P(1|0)

answer: Best threshold: erfc falls extremely fast, so the BER is dominated by whichever tail is larger. Moving I<sub>D</sub> shrinks one tail and grows the other; the BER is (very nearly) smallest when the two arguments are equal: (I<sub>1</sub> − I<sub>D</sub>)/σ<sub>1</sub> = (I<sub>D</sub> − I<sub>0</sub>)/σ<sub>0</sub> = Q.

answer.text: Solving for I<sub>D</sub> and Q:
answer.pre:
σ<sub>0</sub>(I<sub>1</sub> − I<sub>D</sub>) = σ<sub>1</sub>(I<sub>D</sub> − I<sub>0</sub>)  →  I<sub>D</sub> = (σ<sub>0</sub>I<sub>1</sub> + σ<sub>1</sub>I<sub>0</sub>)/(σ<sub>0</sub> + σ<sub>1</sub>)
Q = (I<sub>1</sub> − I<sub>D</sub>)/σ<sub>1</sub> = (I<sub>1</sub> − I<sub>0</sub>)/(σ<sub>1</sub> + σ<sub>0</sub>)
BER = ½[½erfc(Q/√2) + ½erfc(Q/√2)] = ½ erfc(Q/√2) ≈ e<sup>−Q²/2</sup>/(Q√(2π))

answer.text: Reference values:

answer: Midway threshold: I<sub>D</sub> = 0.55 µA. The 1 level is (1.0 − 0.55)/0.10 = 4.5 of its noise widths away, the 0 level (0.55 − 0.10)/0.05 = 9. BER = ½[½erfc(4.5/√2) + ½erfc(9/√2)] = ½[3.40 × 10⁻⁶ + 1.1 × 10⁻¹⁹] = 1.7 × 10⁻⁶.

Evaluation: the midway threshold is about 1700 times worse. Almost all its errors come from the noisy 1 level, while the quiet 0 level has a huge, wasted margin. Moving the threshold towards the quieter level balances the two margins. Searching numerically for the exact minimum gives I<sub>D</sub> = 0.404 µA and a BER only about 6 % lower than at 0.40 µA, so the simple formula is good enough.

When does it happen? σ<sub>1</sub> > σ<sub>0</sub> whenever the noise depends on the signal: shot noise (σ² ∝ I), and most strongly APD noise (σ² ∝ M²F I). In a thermal-noise-limited PIN receiver σ<sub>1</sub> ≈ σ<sub>0</sub> and the midway threshold is right. Practical receivers often adjust the threshold to minimise measured errors.
Check: errors per second at 2.5 Gbit/s are 2.5 × 10⁹ × 9.9 × 10⁻¹⁰ = 2.5 with the best threshold and 2.5 × 10⁹ × 1.7 × 10⁻⁶ = 4250 with the midway one.

bank.q: Compare the low-impedance, high-impedance and transimpedance front ends for noise, bandwidth and dynamic range, taking C<sub>T</sub> = 1 pF and a 2.5 Gbit/s signal that needs a bandwidth of 1.75 GHz. Which would you choose for a 2.5 Gbit/s long-haul link?
outline: low impedance: R<sub>L</sub> = 50 Ω, wide bandwidth, high thermal noise
high impedance: large R<sub>L</sub>, lowest noise, narrow bandwidth, needs an equaliser, poor dynamic range
transimpedance: B ≈ A/(2πR<sub>f</sub>C<sub>T</sub>), R<sub>f</sub> set by the bandwidth
noise √(4k<sub>B</sub>TB/R) for each choice with numbers
TIA about 7.8 dB more sensitive than 50 Ω here
choice: APD or PIN with a TIA, often with an optical preamplifier for long haul
answer: Requirement: the noise of a resistor R over the 1.75 GHz bandwidth is √(4k<sub>B</sub>TB/R), and the sensitivity P<sub>sens</sub> = Qσ/R (R the responsivity) is proportional to that noise. So the aim is the largest effective resistor that still gives 1.75 GHz with C<sub>T</sub> = 1 pF.

Low-impedance front end: R<sub>L</sub> = 50 Ω gives B = 1/(2π × 50 × 10⁻¹²) = 3.18 GHz, more than enough, but the noise is √(4 × 1.38 × 10⁻²³ × 300 × 1.75 × 10⁹/50) = 762 nA rms. Simple and wideband, but the least sensitive.

High-impedance front end: a large R<sub>L</sub>, say 10 kΩ, gives only 54 nA of noise over 1.75 GHz, but its own bandwidth is 1/(2π × 10⁴ × 10⁻¹²) = 15.9 MHz, about 110 times too narrow. An equaliser (differentiator) must restore the response. The integrated signal builds up over long runs of ones, so the amplifier saturates easily: poor dynamic range, and the equaliser must match the front end closely.

Transimpedance front end: with A = 20, B ≈ A/(2πR<sub>f</sub>C<sub>T</sub>), so R<sub>f</sub> = A/(2πBC<sub>T</sub>) = 20/(2π × 1.75 × 10⁹ × 10⁻¹²) = 1.82 kΩ. Its noise is √(4k<sub>B</sub>TB/R<sub>f</sub>) = 126 nA rms. Feedback also keeps the input at a virtual ground, so large signals do not saturate it as quickly: wide dynamic range and no equaliser.

answer.text: Comparison (C<sub>T</sub> = 1 pF, 1.75 GHz, 300 K, amplifier noise ignored):

answer: Sensitivity differences come from P<sub>sens</sub> ∝ σ: 10 log₁₀(762/126) = 7.8 dB and 10 log₁₀(762/54) = 11.5 dB. The high-impedance design looks best on paper, but at 2.5 Gbit/s its equaliser would also boost the amplifier's high-frequency noise, and its overload at long runs of ones is a serious practical problem.
A fourth option, the integrating front end (integrate the current over each bit, sample, then reset), suits low bit rates and burst-mode receivers; it is rarely used at 2.5 Gbit/s.

Choice for 2.5 Gbit/s long haul: a transimpedance front end. It gives most of the high-impedance sensitivity with the full bandwidth and a wide dynamic range, and needs no matched equaliser. For long spans the detector would be an InGaAs APD with a temperature-compensated bias (5 to 10 dB more sensitive than a PIN), or a PIN after an erbium-doped fiber amplifier.
Check: R<sub>f</sub> = 1.82 kΩ with A = 20 and 1 pF gives 20/(2π × 1820 × 10⁻¹²) = 1.75 GHz, and √(4 × 1.38 × 10⁻²³ × 300 × 1.75 × 10⁹/1820) = 126 nA, consistent with the table.

bank.q: A 2.5 Gbit/s link must span 120 km at 1.55 µm with a target BER of 10⁻¹². The transmitter launches 0 dBm; the fiber loses 0.25 dB/km; two connectors lose 0.5 dB each and splices 1.0 dB in total; keep a 3 dB system margin. The receiver has R = 0.9 A/W and a transimpedance front end with σ<sub>T</sub> = 150 nA rms in B = 1.25 GHz. Choose between a PIN and an InGaAs APD (k = 0.5), choose the gain, and justify the design.

answer.text: Power budget:

answer: Q for the target: ½erfc(Q/√2) = 10⁻¹² gives Q = 7.03.

PIN receiver: thermal-noise limited, P<sub>sens</sub> = Qσ<sub>T</sub>/R = 7.03 × 150 × 10⁻⁹/0.9 = 1.17 × 10⁻⁶ W = −29.3 dBm. It needs 5.7 dB more power than the link delivers with margin (−29.3 against −35.0 dBm). The PIN fails; without margin it would still fail by 2.7 dB.

APD receiver: P<sub>sens</sub> = (Q/R)(qFBQ + σ<sub>T</sub>/M) with F = kM + (1 − k)(2 − 1/M) and k = 0.5 for an InGaAs/InP APD. Q/R = 7.82 A⁻¹·W and qBQ = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 1.25 × 10⁹ × 7.03 = 1.41 nA.

answer.text: Sensitivity against gain:

answer: Optimum: M<sub>opt</sub> ≈ √[(σ<sub>T</sub>/(QqB) + k − 1)/k] = √[(106.6 − 0.5)/0.5] = 14.6, giving P<sub>sens</sub> = 171 nW = −37.7 dBm, 8.4 dB better than the PIN.

Gain setting: the curve is flat between M = 10 and M = 20 (within 0.3 dB). Choose M ≈ 10 to 12 rather than the exact optimum: lower M means lower bias (further from breakdown), less multiplied dark current, wider gain–bandwidth margin at 2.5 Gbit/s, and less sensitivity to temperature. At M = 10 the receiver gives −37.4 dBm, 2.4 dB better than the required −35.0 dBm, on top of the 3 dB margin.

Front end and detector: InGaAs/InP SAM APD (InGaAs absorbs at 1.55 µm, InP multiplies) with η giving R = 0.9 A/W, feeding the transimpedance amplifier (its bandwidth A/(2πR<sub>f</sub>C<sub>T</sub>) must cover about 1.75 GHz). A bias supply of a few tens of volts, temperature-compensated or in a gain-control loop, holds M near 10 because V<sub>B</sub> rises with temperature.

Effects to check: dark current (the bulk part is multiplied and adds shot noise 2qI<sub>db</sub>M²FB; it is negligible only while I<sub>db</sub> is far below the average primary photocurrent at sensitivity, 0.9 × 183 nW = 165 nA, which a good InGaAs APD with a few nA meets); dispersion at 1.55 µm over 120 km at 2.5 Gbit/s (standard fiber disperses about 17 ps/(nm·km), so a narrow-linewidth laser is needed and a dispersion penalty must come out of the margin); and the extinction ratio of the transmitter (r<sub>ex</sub> = 0.1 costs about 0.9 dB with thermal noise).

Against the alternatives: the PIN is cheaper and simpler but cannot close this budget. An optical preamplifier (an EDFA) in front of a PIN would give more sensitivity than the APD but costs more and adds its own noise. The quantum limit, about 13.5 photons per bit on average at 10⁻¹² (4.3 nW, −53.6 dBm), shows how far any real receiver is from the ideal: the APD design is 16 dB above it.

Conclusion: use an InGaAs/InP APD with a transimpedance front end at M ≈ 10, sensitivity −37.4 dBm, giving 2.4 dB beyond the 3 dB system margin. Risk: if the temperature control fails and M falls to 5, the sensitivity drops to −35.7 dBm and the spare margin shrinks to 0.7 dB.

glossary.def: A device that turns incident optical power into an electrical current, usually a reverse-biased semiconductor junction.
A p–n junction run in reverse bias so that light-generated electron–hole pairs are swept out as current.
The fraction of incident photons that produce a collected electron–hole pair, written η.
The photocurrent produced per unit incident optical power, in amperes per watt.
The longest wavelength a material can absorb, λ<sub>c</sub> = 1.24/E<sub>g</sub> µm with E<sub>g</sub> in eV.
The small current that flows in a photodiode with no light, from carriers generated by heat in the bulk and leakage along the surface.
The zone of a reverse-biased junction that holds almost no free carriers but a strong electric field.
A photodiode with a wide intrinsic layer between p and n regions, giving high efficiency, fast drift collection and low capacitance.
The time carriers take to cross the depleted layer, w/v<sub>sat</sub>; it limits the photodiode bandwidth.
A photodiode biased near breakdown so that each photon-generated pair triggers a chain of impact ionisations, giving internal gain.
The process in which a fast carrier in a strong field knocks a bound electron free, creating an extra electron–hole pair.
The ratio M of the multiplied output current of an APD to the primary photocurrent.
The factor F ≥ 1 by which the random avalanche raises the shot noise above that of a noiseless gain M.
The ratio k of hole to electron ionisation rates; a small k gives a quieter avalanche.
A separate absorption and multiplication APD: InGaAs absorbs the light and InP multiplies the carriers.
Current noise from the random arrival of individual carriers; its mean square is 2qIB.
Current noise from random thermal motion of electrons in a resistor; its mean square is 4k<sub>B</sub>TB/R.
The optical power that gives a signal equal to the noise (SNR = 1) in a 1 Hz bandwidth, in W/√Hz.
The first amplifier after the photodiode; its noise usually sets the noise of the whole receiver.
A current-to-voltage amplifier with a feedback resistor R<sub>f</sub>; it combines low noise with wide bandwidth.
A filter that corrects the receiver's frequency response so the pulses reach the decision circuit with the right shape.
The comparator that samples the filtered signal once per bit and outputs a 1 or a 0.
The minimum average received optical power that gives the specified BER at the specified bit rate.
The probability that a bit is decided wrongly; errors per second = BER × bit rate.
The ratio (I<sub>1</sub> − I<sub>0</sub>)/(σ<sub>1</sub> + σ<sub>0</sub>) that measures how far apart the two levels are compared with their noise.
An overlay of many received bit periods on an oscilloscope, used to judge noise, jitter and intersymbol interference.
The extra received power, in dB, needed to restore the target BER after an impairment.
The ratio r<sub>ex</sub> = P<sub>0</sub>/P<sub>1</sub> of the power sent for a 0 to the power sent for a 1.
The sensitivity of an ideal noiseless detector: about 10 photons per bit on average for BER = 10⁻⁹.
Optical power relative to 1 mW: P(dBm) = 10 log₁₀(P/1 mW).
